19621.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE6354 : Networked and Multi-agent Control Systems { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction to multi-agent systems, Graph Theory: Graphs and digraphs, Adjacency matrix, Incidence matrix, Laplacian matrix, Edge Laplacian matrix [8]
Module 2 :

Consensus: agreement subspace, convergence analysis, average consensus, Stochastic matrix, Perron-Frobenius results, Primitive matrix, Gersgorin disc theorem, Convergence analysis, Spanning rooted out-branching, Consensus control [8]
Module 3 :

Formation Control: Formation specification, Formation invariants (scale, translation and rotation), Formation control, Rigid framework, Infinitesimal rigidity, Rigidity matrix, Minimally rigid framework, Gradient-based control [8]
Module 4 :

Consensus (General Dynamics): Distributed static state feedback control, Leader-Follower consensus, Distributed output feedback control [6]

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce the fundamental concepts of multi-agent systems (MAS) and their applications in cooperative control, coordination, and distributed decision-making.
2 .

To develop a strong mathematical foundation using graph theory for modelling and analysing the communication topology among interacting agents.
3 .

To understand consensus algorithms and analyse convergence properties using matrix theory, eigenvalue analysis, and stability concepts.
4 .

To study formation control strategies and the role of rigidity theory in maintaining and controlling geometric formations among multiple agents.
5 .

To design distributed control laws for consensus and formation under general agent dynamics, including leader–follower and output feedback scenarios.

Course Outcome

1 .

Model multi-agent systems using graph-theoretic tools such as adjacency, incidence, Laplacian, and edge Laplacian matrices.
2 .

Analyze and ensure consensus in multi-agent networks using stochastic matrices, Perron–Frobenius theory, and convergence analysis techniques.
3 .

Apply Gersgorin’s theorem and algebraic connectivity concepts to evaluate system stability and rate of convergence in distributed coordination problems.
4 .

Design and implement formation control laws based on rigidity theory, gradient-based methods, and formation invariants (translation, rotation, and scaling).
5 .

Develop distributed control strategies for leader–follower and output-feedback-based consensus problems in linear multi-agent systems.

Essential Reading

1 .

Francesco Bullo, Lectures on Network Systems, Kindle Direct Publishing , Edition 1.7, Apr 2024

2 .

W. Ren and R.W. Beard, Distributed Consensus in Multi-vehicle Cooperative Control: Theory and Application, Springer-Verlag , London, 2008

Supplementary Reading

1 .

M. Mesbahi and M. Egerstedt, Graph Theoretic Methods in Multiagent Networks, Princeton University Press , NJ, 2010

Journal and Conferences

1 .

Z. Li, Z. Duan, G. Chen and L. Huang, “Consensus of Multi-agent Systems and Synchronization of Complex Networks: A Unified Viewpoint”, IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems-I: Regular Papers, Vol. 57-1, 2010.
2 .

H. Zhang, F. L. Lewis and A. Das, “Optimal Design for Synchronization of Cooperative Systems: State Feedback, Observer and Output Feedback”, IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, vol. 56, no. 8, 2011.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME6137 : Rotor Dynamics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I
The rotor-shaft system: the disc, the shaft, the bearing and mass unbalance. Symmetric and asymmetric rotor. Flexural vibration, critical speeds and unbalanced response of shaft. Rotor-bearing interaction and effects of anisotropy. [8 hrs.]
Module II
Gyroscopic effects. Effects of axial load and axial torque. Determination of mathematical model: lumped mass approach and equivalent discretized system (finite element model). [8 hrs.]
Module III
Damped rotors, External damping, Internal damping, Stability analysis. [6 hrs.]
Module IV
Geared and branched systems. Rotors mounted in fluid film bearings. Steady state characteristics of bearings. Rigid and flexible rotor balancing. [6 hrs.]
Module V
Dynamics of cracked shafts. Identification of cracks in rotors and other parts through vibration analysis: Condition monitoring. Thermal effects due to vibration of shafts. [8 hrs.]

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to
CO1: Obtain basic ideas about the rotor dynamics theory.
CO2: Enhance the knowledge in some other associated field like modal analysis of vibrating body, cracked structure and condition monitoring.
CO3: Implement the above ideas in the practical field to solve modern engineering problems.
CO4: Design the rotor shaft according to the practical requirement.
CO5: Train the young engineers for health monitoring of rotating machinery.

J. S. Rao, Rotor Dynamics, New Age, New Delhi , Third ed., 1996

2 .

G. Genta, Dynamics of rotating systems, Springer , 2005

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA4114 : Urban Design and Infrastructure { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Introduction to urban design:
Ideologies, characteristics, and scope in urban design role of an urban designer brief description of historical evolution of city morphology context of urbanization and urbanism systems of human settlements and townscapes, concepts of place and place making.
Module II: Reviewing classical texts and theories in urban design:
Works of Camilo Sitte, Le Corbusier, Clarence S Stein, Kevin Lynch, Jane Jacobs, William H Whyte, Colin Rowe, Gordon Cullen, Aldo Rossi, Leslie Martin, Christian Schulz, Rob Krier, Gabriel Feld, and others.
Assignment: Term paper on selected topic related to urban design theories.
Module III: Elements of the city and creation of database:
Understanding the implication of various urban scale element like urban atriums, courtyards, plazas, streets, boulevards, greenways, waterways, riverfronts, beaches, urban farming, pedestrian and bike ways, heritage areas, urban infrastructure, parking lots etc.
Data base for physical surveys including land use, building use, density, building age, etc., and socioeconomic surveys. Sampling and survey techniques. Land use classification or coding Preparation of base maps: concepts of scales, components and detailing for various levels of plans input output analysis, SWOT analysis.
Module IV: Urban infrastructure:
Concepts of urban infrastructure - social, physical, health infrastructure, urban form - size implications for services integration. Infrastructure overlay - services and utilities network - qualitative and quantitative assessment of demand - supply - water supply, sewerage/drainage and waste management, communication and transit networks & urban social infrastructure, infrastructure development financing models and emerging options urban flooding and concept of sponge cities.
Module V: Case studies in urban design:
Analysis of selected case studies based on the aspects covered in Module II, III, IV.
Assignment: Student presentation on case studies.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the factors shaping and developing the form and structure of cities and its overall fabric.
2 .

To understand urban design concepts, its contextual relevance and its multi-disciplinary aspects.
3 .

To understand the methods of analysis and interpretation of urban solutions.

Course Outcome

1 .

Ability to understand fundamental concepts of urban design and its various dimensions and appreciate existing theories and solutions.
Ability to understand complexity, conflicts, and multi-disciplinary aspects of urban design and incorporate the needs of various stakeholders.
Ability to understand strategies and policies, amalgamate theoretical models, analytical approaches and contexts.
Ability to effectively communicate and represent urban design solutions.

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH5106 : Quantum Information and Computing { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

(8 hrs) Motivation for Quantum Technologies, classical vs. quantum computation, linear algebra (vector spaces, inner products, and norms), operators and matrices, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, tensor products, Dirac notation (bra-ket), quantum states, wave-functions, probabilistic interpretation, observables and measurements, projective measurements
Module 2 :

(8 hrs) Quantum state evolution, quantum bits, quantum register, unitary evolution and quantum gates, basics of quantum correlations and superposition, two-qubit systems and Bell states, entanglement and its significance, controlled gates (CNOT, Toffoli, Fredkin).
Module 3 :

(8 hrs) Quantum teleportation, no-cloning theorem, superdense coding, classical error-correcting codes, quantum error-correcting codes, Shor’s 3-qubit bit-flop code, error correction in quantum sustems.
Module 4 :

(8 hrs) Overview and classification of algorithms, problem-solving on quantum computers, basics of Deutsch algorithm, Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm for decision problems, classical vs. quantum speed-up, Grover’s search algorithm, Shor’s factoring algorithm.
Module 5 :

(4 hrs) Principles of information security, classical versus quantum cryptography and key distribution basics, current challenges and future directions in quantum technologies and quantum computing.

Course Objective

1 .

To impart knowledge on
Provide students with foundational knowledge of quantum mechanics, linear algebra, and quantum information science.
2 .

Introduce the principles of quantum computation and the essential differences between classical and quantum systems.
3 .

Introduce algorithms that are simple yet demonstrate quantum speed-up.
4 .

To impart an understanding of quantum information theory, including quantum teleportation, superdense coding, and quantum cryptography.
5 .

Provide understanding of real-world quantum computing technologies.

Course Outcome

1 .

Upon successful completion of the course,
CO1. The students will gain an overall understanding on the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics and their application in quantum computation.
2 .

CO2. The students will obtain knowledge on description and implementation of quantum gates, circuits, and simple quantum algorithms such as Deutsch-Jozsa, Bernstein-Vazirani, and Simon's algorithm.
3 .

CO3. The students will be able to appreciate the significance of quantum correlations in comparison of classical correlations useful for quantum speed-ups.
4 .

CO4. The students will demonstrate knowledge of quantum information protocols, including quantum teleportation, superdense coding, and quantum key distribution.
5 .

CO5. The students will be able to identify and discuss some aspects of physical realizations of quantum computers and their associated challenges.

Essential Reading

1 .

A., & Chuang, I. L., , Quantum Computation and Quantum Information, Cambridge University Press (2010).

2 .

Parag K. Lala, Quantum Computing: A Beginner's Introduction, McGraw-Hill Education, 1st Edition (2019).

Preskill, J., Lecture Notes on Quantum Computation, https://www.lorentz.leidenuniv.nl/quantumcomputers/literature/preskill_1_to_6.pdf.

2 .
